L0: # Rogue V3
L1: 
L2: 【0†RLGallery】 -> 【1†About】 -> Rogue V3
L3: 
L4: This game is a version of UNIX Rogue 3.6.
L5: ## Development History
L6: 
L7: The original Rogue was created about 1980 by Michael Toy and Glenn Wichman, who at that time were students at the University of California, Santa Cruz. Michael Toy later transferred to Berkeley and continued to develop Rogue along with Ken Arnold, creator of the curses library.
L8: Rogue first ran under an early version of the 【2†BSD Unix†en.wikipedia.org】 operating system on the 【3†DEC PDP-11†en.wikipedia.org】 minicomputer. Early in 1981, copies of Rogue began to be included in the 【4†2BSD†en.wikipedia.org】 software collection, which brought it to a wide audience. Version 3.6 was released in April 1981 and became very popular in university computer labs.
L9: Rogue 3.6 is the ancestor of Super-Rogue, Advanced Rogue, and the other early roguelikes. The original authors controlled access to Rogue's source code, mostly to make cheating harder. But sometime around June 1981, an unidentified outsider got hold of a copy. All the other games used this code as a starting point.
L10: ## Restoration
L11: 
L12: Because of the copying incident, the Rogue 3.6 source code could be found in several places on the Internet. The 【5†Roguelike Restoration Project†web.archive.org】 ported the game to run on modern computer systems. The RRP worked from 2000 to 2006, releasing a version called 3.6.3 at the end.
L13: 
L14: The Roguelike Gallery's version is based on the RRP's Rogue 3.6.3. There have been some small modifications in order to work with the Gallery's multi-user environment. A few bugs have also been fixed.
L15: ## More Information

L17: # Zork
L18: 
L19: The Great Underground Empire
L20: 
L21: West of a white house, in an open field, lies the Great Underground Empire: MIT's witty, sarcastic answer to Adventure, home of the lurking grue and the best-selling text adventure of its age.
L22: 
L23: Zork proved that a parser could understand full sentences and that text could carry humor, personality and a coherent world; it launched Infocom, the premier text-adventure studio, and through its Fortran port Dungeon it gave the first MUD its name.
L24: ## Overview
L25: "West of House. You are standing in an open field west of a white house, with a boarded front door." Behind that house lies the Great Underground Empire, a vast, abandoned realm built by the extravagant Lord Dimwit Flathead, where treasure waits among a dam, a coal mine, a volcano, a thief who picks your pockets, and in every unlit passage the grue.
L26: Zork, created at MIT in 1977 and sold by Infocom from 1980 as a trilogy, is the most famous piece of 【19†interactive fiction】 ever written and the adventure game that showed how much personality a text parser could have.
L27: ## Origins
L28: In the spring of 1977, 【20†Colossal Cave Adventure】 was a hit at MIT; by the end of May players had solved it completely. Four members of the Dynamic Modelling Group at MIT's Laboratory for Computer Science, students Tim Anderson, Marc Blank and Bruce Daniels and research staff member Dave Lebling, decided to write a better one, with richer sentences and fairer puzzles. They worked in MDL, a language suited to processing text, on a PDP-10.
L29: Lebling wrote the first parser; while he was on a two-week vacation the others built a prototype, and the file was called "zork," a nonsense word used around the lab for unfinished programs.
L30: Because MIT's machines were open to anyone on the ARPANET, curious users found the game and spread it before it was finished, becoming an informal community of playtesters. The group added grues to replace the pits that killed players in the dark, borrowing the name from 【21†Jack Vance】. Lebling noted that the combat system echoed 【22†Dungeons & Dragons】, though he said his colleagues had never played it, and he thought of the parser as a kind of 【23†Dungeon Master】 narrating the story.
L31: In 1978 DEC employee Bob Supnik ported the game to Fortran, and the team, having renamed it Dungeon, released it under that title through the DEC users group. 【24†TSR】 claimed the name infringed on its trademark, and the authors went back to Zork. The final puzzle went in during February 1979.
L32: ## How it plays
L33: The player types commands, from "north" and "get lamp" to "put the lamp and sword in the case," and the program answers with sardonic, conversational prose. The 1977 version had 32 treasures and an endgame; for home computers it was split into three episodes. In Zork I: The Great Underground Empire, the goal is to find 19 treasures and deposit them in a trophy case in the white house. Zork II: The Wizard of Frobozz adds a wandering, fading wizard whose spells all begin with F and a stronger plot.
L34: Zork III: The Dungeon Master introduces time pressure and ends with the player inheriting the mantle of the Dungeon Master himself. Puzzles can often be solved more than one way, and light is life: without a lamp, "it is pitch black. You are likely to be eaten by a grue."
L35: ## Reception & impact
L36: 
L37: In 1979 Anderson, Blank, Lebling and others founded Infocom. Marc Blank and Joel Berez fitted the huge mainframe game onto microcomputers by designing the Zork Implementation Language and a portable virtual machine, the Z-machine, so one game file could run on many computers. Microsoft passed on publishing, so Personal Software released Zork I for the TRS-80 in December 1980, followed by an Apple II version. Infocom soon self-published and completed the trilogy by the fall of 1982.
L38: Sales grew for years. Zork I sold 38,000 copies by the end of 1982 and around 150,000 in 1984; the three episodes together passed 680,000 copies through 1986, more than a third of Infocom's sales in that period. Byte declared that no advance in the science of Adventure had been "as bold and exciting." Infocom's hint booklets, printed in invisible ink as InvisiClues, became artifacts in themselves.
